Norman Brownlee, Rio 4, May 5, 1961. And Ms. Brownlee has joined us so she can remind us.
I need reminding. I need two minds.
You wanted to say something about your bass.

Yes, I wanted to tell you about a very fine letter that I got from Dr. Sushon. With reference to my old days around the jazz fields in New Orleans. I happened to have been hospitalized when this letter came. And thus a delay in answering his lovely letter. And I wanted him to know that I thought that if they had room for it, I'd hang my old string bass up in the museum.
And I'm sure they'll find room.
You think they can?

They'll probably have rotating exhibits is probably what they'll do. Change them from month to month. I don't know what they're planning. I see. I don't know if you can talk to Harry about it. But I know they have so much stuff. They have Jack Lane's bass drum.

They have Jack, yes. And they have Rap's clarinet too. Rapola's clarinet. He tells me a lot of this in the letter. Which was the most interesting letter to me. And I certainly have to answer his letter. And I imagine qualify for my subscription to the magazine. Well, that's good.
You're going to get that they have good articles.

Well, he asked me about it. And I won't do it. But it's just procrastination. That's the thief of time. And believe me, I am the world's worst on letter writing. But one of these days, I'll send him an epistle. It'll be a little lengthier than a letter. But I fully intend to do so. And I hope it won't. It'll be forthcoming right soon. You might tell him if you will be kind enough, you said you'd call him and let him know about that or let Mr. Harry know about it, about the bass. I caught his show, This Is Your Life. And maybe Billy Kleppinger might remember me during the days of playing with the Invincibles. You might bring that up. And it was during the days that we used to put on, way back there, we put on minstrel shows too. I was quite a minstrel man back in the old days with Bonnie Casey and Dennis Casey and Warren Spawn. Spawn, not Spawn, Warren Spawn. Well, I can't remember Warren's last name right off the bat, but Chester Aikens and Richard Nichols and Joe Ferguson, bank directors and all, you know. We didn't borrow anybody if they wanted to be in the minstrel. And we'd put on a minstrel first part and a little oleo. And then first thing you know, we'd all get on our instruments and play a dance after. And of course, anybody who wanted to stay, we'd charge them a little extra to dance. And we'd have a dance after the minstrel show. We used to put on shows in Laplace and Sorrento and all around Louisiana there. Had a lot of fun out of it and it was quite educational. We met a lot of fine people at the same time. And I used to play a lot for Frank Williams, Mr. Marguerite Clark. He married Marguerite Clark, the famous movie actress, remember. And we used to play up there on Sony at St. Charles. That's where it was.
5120 St. Charles. I worked in that building. Is that right? I catalogued the collection that Doc gave to the library up there.
Is that right?
All those records and stuff.

Well, it was quite a nice home. We played up there many times with my orchestra after theater parties and things like that. He called me as late as 8.30 in the evening, maybe 9 o'clock, asked me if I could get the boys together and come up. We'd do it. We'd get together and go on up and play a job for them. Have a lot of fun at the same time. Did I mention anything about the Owls being on our taping here? Very little.
Very little. Just sort of in-
Monk Smith and Benji White and- I see.
Benji occasionally.

And Young Mackie, Red's brother. Dick. Dick. Dick Mackie. That's right. And what was Earl's last name? Earl Crumb. Earl Crumb, yes. Earl Crumb. Oh, yeah. Well, that was a fine outfit. They used to have a nice band.
There were several outstanding orchestras around besides you, is there?

Oh, yes. Yes, sir. Sure. Why? Well, any place you go in New Orleans, you had a good band. But it looked like we played, the Owls or Brownlee's band would play for so many of the fraternities and sororities of Tulane. And then Loyola, of course, came into the picture after. And we played quite a bit up at Loyola Gym. We played up there very often. And I remember Cupera. You know, part of my work with Wuerline was organizing school bands. And that was my job was the Con Factory too, you see. For years I organized school bands. And then too, in my ability in music, there was an instrument came out that was invented by a Russian scientist, incidentally. The name was Theremin. And I used to demonstrate the Theremin in schools. In fact, I was supposed to go off with RCA people in demonstrating that. I demonstrated the Theremin to Madame Schumann-Heinck.
Is that right?

Yes. And that same day, I think Madame Schumann-Heinck gave an audition, as it was, to Marian Anderson, a colored woman, very fine voice, very fine person. And I used to play numbers like The Rosary and Because and numbers like that on the theremin. I guess old Johnny Hyman would remember that. Johnny, Johnny used to play around with it too, where it was Wuerlines.
I didn't know that.

Yes. And that was quite an instrument. I don't think that it lasted very long as a musical instrument to be sold in homes, but it was a fad. And it was to do. It was built on the basis of a radio chassis, and it had an upper vertical rod for your tones, and it had a parallel looped bar rod like for your expression with your left hand. And then you played it either with the point of a finger, or I played mine with the side and tip of my little finger. It was like that. And you knew the expressions were this way. And it had the voice of a cello and a violin. It was a very fine instrument.
You know, something I'm about to forget is, how did you happen to make that record anyway?
You mean the record with...
With OK. How did they have to locate you?

Well, they were coming around. They were picking up bands in different locales, different cities. And at that time, my band wasn't the only one that recorded for OK. They made up bands all around New Orleans. Johnny Detroit and Paul and all of them, they made a record with OK then. That was in 1923. I do remember that. I think Johnny made Tulane Swing.
I think that must have been the same time that Papa Celestan and Bebe Ridgely recorded. Just about. They made a record.
They may have made a record then. I didn't think so, but they may have.
It was on OK that they made it.

Did they make it on OK? Well, then they made it at that time. And they made it, you see, we made them up in the Kimbell Piano Corporation, Piano Company, which was above the store. At one time, the Kahn Music Company and Kimbell were part of the same building. See? And then Kimbell had part of the downstairs floor on Carondelet Street, 123 Carondelet, I believe it was, right back of, in those days, Feebleman's.
I know Jimmy Feebleman from that family. I had dinner with him the other night.
Is that right? Is that right? Well, then we had our warehouse and repair department on the fourth floor of that building. And then the third and second and first floor were Kimbell Piano's.
Oh, I know what I wanted to ask you. Who were the saxophones on your record?

Oh, Harold Geordie. He played a sobbing saxophone on one side. Funny part about that was that I said sobbing. At that same time, or right after that, we called it a sobbing. I told Harold that I thought he played a sad saxophone on one side, and I might call it a sobbing saxophone chorus that he took.
Which kind of saxophone?
A tenor. Tenor. And Harry Shields played it. He played what? He played clarinet.
There's a baritone in there, a bass, too.

A bass, I guess it is. Billy Eastwood, I think, played that. I think Billy played. He played banjo and the bass on it, I think. Or Geordie might have played it. I can't exactly recall now. Somebody switched around on something.
Might have been Shields, too.
Yes. Shields was playing. I think it was Harry. Harry Shields that did that.
Did you know a fellow named Martin that played saxophone?
Oh, I knew Martin that played saxophone, yes. I did.
I forgot his first name.

But I had a fellow played with me by the name of Martin. I can recall now when I was playing piano he played saxophone with me. A fellow named Martin. And then right after he left me, he went with, oh, what is this fellow's name? He used to play Meyer Davis. Meyer Davis. Not Meyer Davis, but, well, it was Meyer Davis and this other name. He comes to Pensacola all the time. We went over to Mobile one time and he played over there.
Oh, let me see. Jan Garber? Jan Garber.
Garber Davis, you see, it was years ago.
I was Garber Davis.

But Jan Garber, this friend of mine, Martin, his home originally was Sarasota, Florida. And after he left me, he went with Jan Garber and he played with him about 11 or 12, maybe 14 years. The last I remember that I had seen him. And he was still with Garber. Very fine man.
Let's see, you had a trumpet too on the records.

I don't think that was Sharky. For some reason, I don't think Sharky. Yes, he was too. Sharky. Sharky made the record. Because we got our names on the numbers. They were mine. Dirty, rag and peculiar. But we put three names, I think, on that. Banana, Brownlee and Shields. I believe that was it. I'm pretty sure that's the way it is on there. Yeah, we put it on there.
They were your numbers, huh?
Yeah.
And you had a bass player, I guess, huh? Maybe that's it.
Yeah. No. No bass? No, I don't, no. We didn't use bass. Drummer? Yeah, it's Crumbie. Alonzo.
And banjo?
Yeah, Billy Eastwood. Billy Eastwood was on there.
Who was Berman French?

Berman French was my brother-in-law. He played with me a while. He played banjo too. Of my first marriage. He was my brother-in-law. Incidentally, from my first marriage, Dr. Lochte was married to my sister-in-law from my first marriage. And he was Emmet Hardy's doctor. See, Emmet developed tuberculosis and Dr. Lochte had done so well with a couple of boys that worked for Canal Bank, I think it was. And he did such a fine job with them. He had those boys out playing baseball again in two years. Henry, Dr. Lochte was, he got to be quite a heart and lung specialist for the government, I think, before his passing. And he went back in the service with the rank of Colonel at the Veterans Hospital in Biloxi over there. And, uh, Berman played for a short while. I don't know just how long he played. But he got to be pretty good. He got to be alright.
Oh, uh, your father played in these brass bands. Did they ever play any funerals? Well, I wouldn't know that.

That was before my time. See, I'm the baby of our family. And, uh... Thought of that? Well, no, no. I was in the music business before my father died. But, uh, I was in the hospital with a fever, sick, when he passed away. And I didn't even know it till after his passing. Uh, I was out at the Yacht Club playing a job one night. And I, uh, just passed out on the piano stool. And they brought me to the Naval Hospital in Algiers. And I guess I was in there 30 days before I ever knew anything would happen after it. Yeah, I was in a tough spot. I don't know whether it was typhoid or typhus. And they never could find out. But from that day on, I was never sick. After they got me out of there. Uh, I wasn't sick until here in 1949.
Did you, uh, ever hear any of these bands over there playing any funerals?

Oh, yes. It was nothing. I mean, I just never, uh, in Algiers, oh definitely, because you see everybody walked to the cemeteries in Algiers in those days. They had the, they had the carriages, you know. Yeah. But, uh, people walked to the funerals alongside of the funeral, going.
They'd have, would they have white bands playing the funerals?
Sometimes, yes.
You know, they'd make so much of the colored bands playing them and...

Oh, sure. They had many white bands playing. But now, if you ask me the names of them, uh, I would say that maybe the Wooden of the World or some organization similar to that had, uh, had bands. Did they play any jazzies? No, no, they just, they played the dirge. They played a funeral dirge. Uh-huh. Uh, it was, it was the colored bands, really, that, uh, came back, uh, rejoicing from, from the, from the last resting place of their friend. But, uh, I guess the, I guess it's traditional with them. The other bands would pack up and ride home or walk home.
What about, uh, Frankie Doosan, the colored trombone player from Al Jaze? Did you ever hear him? I just wondered.
Doosan?
Doosan.
Doosan.
Frankie Doosan.
It must be since my time, huh? Or how, how, is he an old timer?
Well, he was playing around 1900.
Mm.
And he played on up.

I'm sure you heard him. Well, it might be just, I, I, no doubt I heard him, just like I was talking about Kid Thomas and I was talking about somebody else. Uh. Peter Volcage. Well, Peter Volcage, yeah, well, he was, he was all right. And then there used to be a violinist, too, that was quite a, one of them that lived in Al Jaze, he was similar to this left-hand violin player in the Lyric Theater and-
Robichaux?
Robichaux. He played style like he did. He was very good.
Where did he live that they called the violin player, do you remember?
Well, he lived somewhere in Al Jaze, whether, whether, whether- Charlie DeVergis. DeVergis. Charlie DeVergis.
And Professor Minetta, who talked about him.
Well, yeah, Al Minetta, yeah. He played violin. He played violin, played well. And Bocas played violin, too. Yeah, I was going to say, I thought that Pete played violin as well. Still does. Uh-huh.

And do you know Charlie Love? He's a trumpet player from all that college, you know what, anyway? I don't remember. He and Bocas made some records where Bocas plays the violin and Love plays the trumpet. And they played some of the Red Book ragtime arrangements like Maple Leaf and-

What was the name of this violin player that used to play out at Tranchinas years ago? Piron. Piron. I'll never forget, Piron recorded a number that an old friend of mine wrote. I used to write some tunes with him. Joe Burgess and- Oh, yeah. I know Joe Burgess. Jimmy Dupree. Jimmy Dupree and I used to write songs together.
Joe was still playing. I run into him once in a while.
Is that right?
I love Don't Leave Me Daddy.

Well, that was one of them. Jimmy Dupree wrote Jelly Bean, too, you remember? And he used to work for Feist. Joe goes up to New York and Jimmy and I were sitting around the Elks Club in New Orleans there and we wrote a number. My cozy little blue room. In a cozy little blue room. And it was similar on a show type number. And Joe writes down, he says, I sold my half to Phil Kornheiser and Feist. What you all gonna do with your half? Two more of us, our half. He sold his half. Jimmy said, the nerve of him. How big does he think he is? He's just a half pint as it is. But Jimmy Dupree wrote a number that he sold to P. Ronheiser. It's called My Purple Rose of Cairo.
Oh, that's beautiful.
You gotta be a dope fiend to think of a title like that. And Jimmy wrote all that? Sure Jimmy wrote that number. And he just sold it to P. Ronheiser.
I don't think P. Ronheiser ever wrote any music.
Oh, I guess he had the ability to. He was pretty good.
I don't know. Pete Bocard told me he wrote all the music and P. Ronheiser wrote the work.
Oh, is that it? Yeah.
And Louie's supposed to have written...

I don't like to discredit anyone. No, I don't either. I didn't say that about Dupree either. But Dupree had such an imaginative mind. I've never seen anybody or met anybody like him. He was up in New York one time. Well, for instance, he came through here and he used to get letters and mail and everything. I think a lot of times he'd write himself letters and read them. He was quite a character and I often wonder what happened to him.
I don't know.
He got to be a member of the Society of Composers and Publishers. I do know that.
But he left New Orleans.
ASCAP. And of course Joe, Joe got to be a member of ASCAP also.
I wanted to ask you about who some of your favorite banjo players were back in those times.

Well, I liked Jules. He was fine. And Billy Eastwood was very good. Billy tuned his banjo. Now, Billy could play both tunings. But Billy tuned his banjo ukulele styling. And that's why he and Pinkertour had quite an argument one time. And so Pinkertour says, all right, all right. He put up a piece of music. He says, for instance, he says, now with that tuning you can't play this piece. He says, here's a piece. Play this piece. And he put it up there and Billy took the piece and he just took his banjo and played it right off. He could read, see.
Oh.

And that was so astounding that I have never seen Paul Whiteman's stomach shake so, you know, all my life. A laugh. You know, if you could get anything on anybody, old Pops would, he'd stand back there and he'd really give you a big belly laugh, in other words. He had the equipment. Oh, he had the equipment. And he'd really, he'd really, he was a wonderful person. And like when Snoozer Quinn, he came backstage at St. Charles Theatre. And Snoozer could play, you know, play without, play with his fingers on the, on the, on the frets, you see. Without, without stroking the strings in some of the passages, you see. And so I said, Snoozer, I want you to shake hands with Mr. Whiteman. He says, glad to know you Mr. Whiteman with that, with that head to one side, you know. And he kept on playing. And Paul, Paul caught it that quick and got a big bang out of it. And he said, wait a minute, wait a minute, keep on playing, I'll be right back, see. Keep on playing, I'll be right back. And he went to get Pinkertore, see. And he brought Mike over there and he says, Mike, I want you to meet Snoozer Quinn. And he says, glad to know you Mr. Pinkertore. And he kept on playing, you see. Shaking hands with Pinkertore and he was still playing. Well that was brand new to Paul, see. And man, he was, he said, keep on, keep on. And he went and got this piano player, wonderful person. Roy Boygie. Roy Boygie, yeah, yeah. And Harry McDonald and all that bunch of around Snoozer. Well I'll tell you what actually happened with Snoozer. Snoozer had to come home. Snoozer was from a little town in Bogalusa, Louisiana. I know. You know him, huh? Well I know people from over there used to live near him. And Snoozer was, he went up there and Paul had Snoozer on party. More than he had him in the band. He'd go around with Paul and all, partying at night with Jimmy Walker and that bunch up in New York. And pretty near kill Snoozer had to come home or he'd have died. It's hard to hold the pace with some of those fellas. Oh yeah. But really, a lot of the things in the music business that I've been around, people that I've known. I've enjoyed them all. But like I say, music has been an avocation. I could always respect the... I got to playing music steady after the Depression, during the Depression. Of course we got a few mules when we were out there playing sometimes. I never shall forget we went to play the Silver Slipper in Memphis. And Eddie Miller and Badouk and Ben Pollock and Goodman and all that. Not Ben, but his brother plays bass came through.
Yeah.

I forget his first name. Harry, I think it was. Yeah. Harry Goodman. And they all came in. They came up. We were staying at the Claridge Hotel there in Memphis. And they all came through. They had had thirteen mules on the way from the west coast coming over trying to get back to New York.
What's a mule now?

A mule is where you play all night and the man just didn't take in the money. Yeah. Didn't take in enough to pay you. Pay you everything. What were you going to do? It was times when, so what? Kill me. You know? See for yourself. Yeah, that's right. What you want, blood? Yeah. Oh, man. Why did you quit playing?
Huh?

Why did you quit playing? Well, like I was about to say, music has been an avocation with me more than for steady fare. And I have been successful. Like I came here on, the boys had never been out on the road with Geordie. And Mr. Pace here in Pensacola wanted us to come over here and play at Florida Town. So the band came over here under the name of Harold Geordie. But when Dave Johnson, a lot of them saw the band, they said, well, that's Norman Brownlee's band from New Orleans. Well, the thing was, a lot of the boys didn't want to go out on the road for the first time with Geordie. They knew that when they were with me, that I got them and managed them well and looked after their welfare pretty well. And they didn't know just how they'd fare with Harold, because he hadn't taken a band out before. Not that he wasn't capable or not that he wasn't a good person. But the fellas just kind of, they just, they said if I'd go, they'd go. So we had nothing else to do, my brother, so we came over here. And now you can't drag me away. I've been here ever since then. I got a job as a rodman and chainman with the engineering gang in CWA. And from that I argued out with the administrator here about setting up a warehouse and setting up projects to house some of the materials and charge it out. And I got to be a warehouseman and bookkeeper. And from there I got into a line that I was definitely proficient in, and that was personnel. And when I got into that I finally got to be assignment officer, and I wound up as district director of employment in charge of sixteen counties, so I didn't do bad in this spot. And I say be a musician or a laborer or what not. If a fella just goes into a community and behaves himself, he'll get along all right. And I've done well in Pensacola, and I guess I'm president of the union here. Did you want to hear anything like that? You didn't want my life's history, did you?
Well, yeah, that's what we're here for.
Oh.
In this remaining minute of the tape.

I do have a minute. Well, from being interested in welfare work, I'm a member of the welfare board in the northwest portion of Florida. I, like I told you, I'm in the cemetery business here, doing all right. And secretary of rotary. And I'd say up to now, no hits, no runs, no errors.
I'm afraid that's about it. I sure have enjoyed it. This has been one of the finest interviews I think we've gotten.
Oh, man. Thank you very much. It's been a pleasure to have you, Dick. We'll let it run off now.
All right.

segments.chapter: Opening and Algiers youth
segments.title: Opening and the Invincibles; Brownlee's orchestra members
segments.summary: Interview opens with name, place and date (Pensacola, 5 May 1961). Brownlee names Invincibles members and sidemen in his own orchestra, with stories of the sax section and a fired saxophonist.

segments.chapter: Opening and Algiers youth
segments.title: Born in Algiers: the family homes
segments.summary: Born 7 Feb 1896 in Algiers; he gives his street addresses and describes the house with its cupola damaged in the 1915 storm.

segments.chapter: Opening and Algiers youth
segments.title: Father's brass band, family music and learning to fake
segments.summary: His father played baritone in the Algiers brass band and held musical evenings at home; the whole family played piano. Brownlee always faked, later learning to read cornet and string bass.

segments.chapter: Early band, Emmett Hardy and Werlein's
segments.title: The jazz club, the Tulane project and Werlein's
segments.summary: Talk about the New Orleans Jazz Club and museum versus the Tulane archive, Pensacola members such as Sterling Turner, and his work with Werlein's music department.

segments.chapter: Early band, Emmett Hardy and Werlein's
segments.title: Oscar Marcour, Joe Lorcanna and Alonzo Crumby in his band
segments.summary: He recalls violinist Oscar Marcour, trombonist/bassist Joe Lorcanna, and drummer Alonzo Crumby, whose steady tempo and band-first attitude he praises.

segments.chapter: Early band, Emmett Hardy and Werlein's
segments.title: The homemade Edison record, Emmett Hardy, Bix and Whiteman
segments.summary: Brownlee describes the home recording with Hardy, Marcour, Eastwood and Crumby, Hardy's wow-wow cornet and influence on Bix, then Walter Holzhaus joining Whiteman and Snoozer Quinn.

segments.chapter: Early band, Emmett Hardy and Werlein's
segments.title: Mickey Marcour and the Brunies family; Rappolo's foolishness
segments.summary: Reminiscing about departed colleagues: Mickey Marcour at the Halfway House, Brunies family news, and a funny Friars Inn argument between Rappolo and another musician.

segments.chapter: Early band, Emmett Hardy and Werlein's
segments.title: Rappolo's humour and Harry Shields's low-register clarinet
segments.summary: Brownlee says Rappolo had a sense of humour but argues Harry Shields first played low-register clarinet; he tells the story of Larry Shields passing the union exam.

segments.chapter: Early band, Emmett Hardy and Werlein's
segments.title: Shields's harmony and Sidney Arodin's Lazy River
segments.summary: Short exchange praising Shields's harmonic ideas and Sidney Arodin as originator of Lazy River, put over by Hoagy Carmichael.

segments.chapter: Early band, Emmett Hardy and Werlein's
segments.title: Bands Brownlee heard growing up in Algiers
segments.summary: Early marching bands and orchestras in Algiers (Babs, Kid Thomas, Henry Allen) and a new Riverside anthology of old New Orleans bands.

segments.chapter: Early band, Emmett Hardy and Werlein's
segments.title: The OK record and the Dorseys' swing band claim
segments.summary: How Brownlee's band made one test and a master that earned about $600, and the Dorseys' claim that he had America's first swing band.

segments.chapter: Depression years and New Orleans trumpeters
segments.title: Jules Baduc's band and Doc Rando
segments.summary: Jules Baduc played banjo and led a band at the Little Club; Henry Rando sang, and Doc Rando went on from medicine or dentistry to play with Crosby and serve on a union board.

segments.chapter: Depression years and New Orleans trumpeters
segments.title: Spot work, then going broke in 1929
segments.summary: His sidemen played with him for spot work; steady engagements came only with the Depression. He lost his money in 1929 managing Atlanta's Con Corporation, then went back to New Orleans.

segments.chapter: Depression years and New Orleans trumpeters
segments.title: Bea Palmer, the shimmy queen
segments.summary: Brownlee identifies Bea Palmer as the shimmy queen Emmett played for at Friars in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Depression years and New Orleans trumpeters
segments.title: His father's law training and Brownlee's choice of music
segments.summary: Brownlee says his father studied law at Tulane, but music was more attractive to him, and the two men compare family professions.

segments.chapter: Depression years and New Orleans trumpeters
segments.title: Professions and the interviewer's own path
segments.summary: Small talk about musicians who worked through college, the interviewer's pre-med years and arrival in New Orleans in 1945 with Monk Hazel, and first hearing Harry Shields.

segments.chapter: Depression years and New Orleans trumpeters
segments.title: Johnny Cotrera and Sharkey Bonano
segments.summary: Brownlee comments on Johnny Cotrera's strong playing and possible resemblance to Sharkey, and on Sharkey's circuit of Blue Room and Vegas work.

segments.chapter: Depression years and New Orleans trumpeters
segments.title: Did Emmett Hardy use a mute? Turk Rene
segments.summary: After a mention of a tape, they discuss whether Hardy used a mute for wah-wah effects and Brownlee praises trumpeter Turk Rene.

segments.chapter: Depression years and New Orleans trumpeters
segments.title: Manuel Moneta, Turk Rene's range and Al Hirt
segments.summary: The interviewer took lessons from Manuel Moneta, who taught Hardy and Rene. Brownlee describes Rene's reading and high notes, and compares Al Hirt's range.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, Eddie Miller and band stories
segments.title: Eureka Brass Band, Pete Bocage and Algiers neighbours
segments.summary: Talk of seeing Pete Bocage play with the Eureka band and where Bocage, Kid Ory and other Black musicians lived in Algiers.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, Eddie Miller and band stories
segments.title: Eddie Miller and Ray Baduc
segments.summary: Brownlee praises the professional dignity of Eddie Miller and Ray Baduc; the interviewer recalls first meeting Miller in a record shop.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, Eddie Miller and band stories
segments.title: Who replaced Emmett Hardy: George Barth and Sharkey
segments.summary: George Barth took Hardy's trumpet chair in Brownlee's band, and Sharkey came in after him.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, Eddie Miller and band stories
segments.title: Billy Braun and the Spinsters Ball in Biloxi
segments.summary: Story of a carnival ball in Biloxi where a novelty band upstaged Brownlee's seasoned band until Ray Baduc's dance saved the night; his advice to do something besides play.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, Eddie Miller and band stories
segments.title: Eddie Edwards and the Original Dixieland Jazz Band
segments.summary: A letter from Eddie Edwards leads to memories of knowing Edwards and drummer Sbarbaro, seen in Miami advertised with the ODJB.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, Eddie Miller and band stories
segments.title: Tom Brown/Ricky Tom and a Whiteman trombonist
segments.summary: Brownlee cannot place a trombonist the interviewer asks about, and tries to recall another trombonist who played years with Whiteman and passed through Pensacola.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, Eddie Miller and band stories
segments.title: Sharkey's tribute at the Dream Room
segments.summary: Brownlee hears Goldie with Jack Teagarden and tells how Sharkey stopped the band to announce him at the Dream Room.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, Eddie Miller and band stories
segments.title: Anton Lada, the Louisiana Five and Tony Parenti
segments.summary: Discussion of Anton Lada, Yellow Nunez and the Louisiana Five at the Tokyo Club, and Brownlee's years of working day and night while music was an avocation.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, Eddie Miller and band stories
segments.title: Howard Voorhees and Louis Armstrong's lip
segments.summary: Brownlee recalls Howard Voorhees helping Armstrong with a no-pressure mouthpiece system, and Armstrong's rise from the Waif's Home.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, Eddie Miller and band stories
segments.title: The Invincibles, Doc Souchon and New Orleans versus Chicago jazz
segments.summary: Brownlee refers the Invincibles' instrumentation to Dr. Souchon, and recalls his This Is Your Life appearance and Eddie Condon's quip about New Orleans and Chicago jazz.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, Eddie Miller and band stories
segments.title: Mike Kaplan and Brownlee's Masonic ties
segments.summary: Mike Kaplan's kindness and Shrine band playing, and Brownlee's own Shrine and Masonic activity.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, Eddie Miller and band stories
segments.title: How Brownlee started on cornet; end of first tape
segments.summary: He picked up cornet with no teacher and reads, in his words, by spelling; the tape runs out.

segments.chapter: Favorite players: trumpet, piano, drums
segments.title: Second tape opening
segments.summary: Tape two begins; Mrs. Brownlee brings refreshments.

segments.chapter: Favorite players: trumpet, piano, drums
segments.title: Sharkey as favourite: the working showman
segments.summary: Brownlee chooses Sharkey as an outstanding musician who worked hard and entertained, doing more than just playing.

segments.chapter: Favorite players: trumpet, piano, drums
segments.title: Playing string bass, and shanghaiing Wingy Manone
segments.summary: Brownlee swung the string bass until his leg stopped him; he tells how his band picked up Wingy Manone off Canal Street when Emmett Hardy was sick.

segments.chapter: Favorite players: trumpet, piano, drums
segments.title: Other trumpet players; Gene Villar and the Bourbon Street Six
segments.summary: He likes George Barth, McPartland and Hackett, and describes his brother-in-law Gene Villar's Dixieland band, Frank Bruno and Frank Horne's tapes.

segments.chapter: Favorite players: trumpet, piano, drums
segments.title: Emmett Hardy, Walter Holzhaus and Charlie Teagarden
segments.summary: Brownlee rates Hardy and Walter Holzhaus (from San Antonio, who could play two tones at once) and mentions Charlie Teagarden and Ray Baduc with Jimmy Dorsey.

segments.chapter: Favorite players: trumpet, piano, drums
segments.title: Frank Froeba, the piano player Fletcher Henderson admired
segments.summary: Brownlee names Frank Froeba as one of the greatest pianists, able to play jazz and orchestra, with honky-tonk piano recordings.

segments.chapter: Favorite players: trumpet, piano, drums
segments.title: The four-piece combo at the Ritz and pianist Frank Panera
segments.summary: A small combo at Jimmy Moran's Ritz with Pinky Gerbrek and Monk Hazel; they try to recall the pianist, eventually Frank Panera.

segments.chapter: Favorite players: trumpet, piano, drums
segments.title: Louis Prima, Leon Prima and Red Bowman
segments.summary: Louis Prima's warm greeting in Pensacola, praise for his trumpet playing, and Red Bowman and Leon Prima as a trumpet pair.

segments.chapter: Favorite players: trumpet, piano, drums
segments.title: Leon Prima's band and drummer Bob Stein
segments.summary: Where Leon's band played around New Orleans, and drummer Bob Stein of Moose Hall.

segments.chapter: Favorite players: trumpet, piano, drums
segments.title: Monk Hazel and the gong on a Brunswick record
segments.summary: Brownlee praises Monk Hazel's drumming and tells how he threw a mallet to hit the gong in time on a Brunswick recording.

segments.chapter: Favorite players: trumpet, piano, drums
segments.title: Charlie Spivak and Frank Horne's coffee sessions
segments.summary: Charlie Spivak and his band visit Pensacola and gather at Frank Horne's house, where Spivak asks Brownlee about old-timers.

segments.chapter: Favorite players: trumpet, piano, drums
segments.title: Leo Adde and Von Gammon
segments.summary: Leo Adde as a fine drummer and reader, and Von Gammon's long engagement at the Grand Hotel.

segments.chapter: Favorite players: trumpet, piano, drums
segments.title: Buck Banville's long run and the sound of small bands
segments.summary: The interviewer describes Buck Banville's band at the American Legion dance and its Halfway House sound; Brownlee notes what seven men can do.

segments.chapter: Reed players and small bands
segments.title: Favorite clarinetists: Tony Parenti and Harry Shields
segments.summary: Brownlee praises Tony Parenti's pit work and use of one clarinet, and Shields's harmonic sense and how players once worked without reading.

segments.chapter: Reed players and small bands
segments.title: The Five Aces, Bob Sackman and Curly Lizano
segments.summary: Brownlee recalls the Five Aces, Bob Sackman's saxophone band, Curly Lizano in Pensacola and a small Tulane pianist who filled in.

segments.chapter: Reed players and small bands
segments.title: Time check and joking about the interviewer's date
segments.summary: Brownlee asks whether he is taking too much time; light banter.

segments.chapter: Reed players and small bands
segments.title: Early New Orleans saxophone players
segments.summary: Johnny Reininger, Howard Reed and Al Galadoro, and an Italian saxophonist whose father Brownlee sold instruments to.

segments.chapter: Owls, Werlein's and the OK record
segments.title: Dr. Souchon's letter and hanging his bass in the museum
segments.summary: Tape three: Brownlee wants to hang his old string bass in the jazz museum and talks about the letter and the museum's holdings.

segments.chapter: Owls, Werlein's and the OK record
segments.title: Minstrel shows and playing for Frank Williams
segments.summary: He recalls the minstrel shows with dances afterward, in Laplace and Sorrento, and playing at the home of Marguerite Clark's husband on St. Charles.

segments.chapter: Owls, Werlein's and the OK record
segments.title: The Owls and other New Orleans orchestras
segments.summary: Brownlee names members of the Owls, another good New Orleans orchestra, and notes there were many good bands.

segments.chapter: Owls, Werlein's and the OK record
segments.title: School bands, Tulane dances and the theremin
segments.summary: His band played fraternity dances; for Werlein's he organized school bands and demonstrated the theremin, including for Madame Schumann-Heink.

segments.chapter: Owls, Werlein's and the OK record
segments.title: How the OK record came about at Kimball's
segments.summary: OK recorders picked up local bands in 1923; Brownlee describes recording above the Kimball piano store on Carondelet Street.

segments.chapter: Owls, Werlein's and the OK record
segments.title: Reed players on the record: Geordie's sobbing sax and Shields
segments.summary: Who played tenor, clarinet and bass sax on the record, including Harold Geordie's sobbing saxophone chorus.

segments.chapter: Owls, Werlein's and the OK record
segments.title: Martin the saxophonist and Jan Garber
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about a saxophonist named Martin, who played for Brownlee and then many years with Jan Garber.

segments.chapter: Owls, Werlein's and the OK record
segments.title: Credits and personnel on the record: Dirty Rag
segments.summary: Sharkey on trumpet, writing credits to Bonano, Brownlee and Shields, no bass, Crumby on drums, Eastwood on banjo.

segments.chapter: Owls, Werlein's and the OK record
segments.title: Berman French and Dr. Lochte, Hardy's doctor
segments.summary: His brother-in-law Berman French played banjo; Dr. Lochte, who treated Hardy's tuberculosis, was married to his sister-in-law.

segments.chapter: Algiers funerals, violinists and songwriters
segments.title: Funerals and bands in Algiers
segments.summary: Funeral processions in Algiers; white bands played dirges only, while Black bands played joyfully on the return.

segments.chapter: Algiers funerals, violinists and songwriters
segments.title: Frankie Dusen, Algiers violinists, Robichaux and Bocage
segments.summary: Brownlee does not know Dusen, then recalls violinists Robichaux, Charlie Devergis, Al Minetta and Pete Bocage, and the Charlie Love records.

segments.chapter: Algiers funerals, violinists and songwriters
segments.title: Songwriting with Jimmy Dupree and Joe Verges
segments.summary: He wrote tunes with Jimmy Dupree and Joe Verges; he tells of selling songs to Feist and doubts about who wrote what, Dupree's eccentricity and ASCAP.

segments.chapter: Banjo, Depression and Pensacola
segments.title: Banjo players, Billy Eastwood and Snoozer Quinn with Whiteman
segments.summary: Billy Eastwood's banjo tuning argument with Pinkerton, Whiteman's laughter, and Snoozer Quinn meeting Whiteman backstage and his time on tour.

segments.chapter: Banjo, Depression and Pensacola
segments.title: The Silver Slipper in Memphis and what a mule is
segments.summary: Meeting Eddie Miller, Baduc and the Goodman band at the Claridge Hotel in Memphis; he explains a mule, a night's pay lost.

segments.chapter: Banjo, Depression and Pensacola
segments.title: Why he quit playing and his move to Pensacola
segments.summary: Music was an avocation; he brought a band to Florida Town, stayed in Pensacola, and rose from CWA work to district director of employment.

segments.chapter: Banjo, Depression and Pensacola
segments.title: Current activities and closing of the interview
segments.summary: He lists his welfare board, cemetery and Rotary work; the interviewer thanks him and the tape ends.
